families.source: UKHSA measles guidance for cases linked to international travel
families.topic: measles risk assessment and contact management for air, sea and land travel
families.page_title: Measles: guidance for Health Protection Teams on cases linked to international travel including air, sea and land crossings
evidence_points: The guidance is intended for health protection teams managing measles cases linked to international travel.
It covers air, sea and land crossing contexts.
It sets out public-health management principles for travel-linked cases.
It includes a contact-tracing evidence review.
It describes recording travel-related contexts in the case management system.
It includes processes for reporting measles associated with international air travel.
It provides sample warn-and-inform communications for passengers or transport staff.
The guidance was updated in January 2026.
Presence on the same journey does not automatically establish a meaningful measles exposure.
Contact tracing and prophylaxis decisions require infectious timing, journey context, susceptibility and current national guidance.

families.topic: immunisation review, infection control and management of suspected diphtheria in migrants
evidence_points: The migrant health guide identifies immunisation and infection prevention as central diphtheria controls.
An immunisation history should be obtained for migrants during assessment.
People with uncertain or incomplete immunisation should be brought up to date under the UK schedule.
Immunisation status of staff and healthcare workers involved in care of recent arrivals should also be reviewed.
The page links to guidance for suspected cases, close contacts and environmental management.
It links to supplementary diphtheria guidance for asylum seeker accommodation.
It identifies resources on skin lesions of public-health importance in newly arrived migrants.
The page was revised in July 2026.
Migrant or arrival status alone does not establish diphtheria infection or exposure.
Action requires individual symptoms, skin findings, immunisation history, exposure and laboratory assessment.

families.source: UKHSA meningococcal carriage and infection technical background
families.topic: carriage prevalence, transmission, invasive disease progression and vaccination effects
families.page_title: Meningococcal carriage and infection: technical background
evidence_points: The technical guidance states that meningococcal carriage is common in young adults.
It reports that approximately 5% to 10% of young adults may carry meningococcal bacteria.
Invasive meningococcal disease is rare but can be severe and fast-moving.
Young adults are important in transmission dynamics even though they do not have the highest absolute disease burden.
Carriage usually occurs in the back of the nose or throat without illness.
Invasive disease occurs when bacteria rarely breach the mucosal barrier and enter the bloodstream.
Dense social environments such as universities are relevant to carriage and transmission.
Adolescent MenACWY vaccination can reduce carriage and contribute to herd protection.
Carriage does not mean that a person has invasive meningococcal disease.
This technical background supplements and does not replace urgent clinical and public-health management guidance.

families.source: UKHSA public health management of toxigenic Corynebacterium ulcerans in companion animals
families.topic: animal index cases, zoonotic risk, toxigenicity testing and human or animal contact management
families.page_title: Public health management of toxigenic C. ulcerans in companion animals
evidence_points: The guidance applies to public-health management of toxigenic Corynebacterium ulcerans in companion animals in England.
It covers investigation needed to confirm toxigenic infection in an animal index case.
It addresses management of the animal and its human and animal close contacts.
Response may require multiagency working between UKHSA, NHS and the Animal and Plant Health Agency.
Potential animal isolates require confirmation and toxigenicity assessment by the relevant reference laboratory.
Companion-animal exposure can be relevant to human toxigenic C. ulcerans infection.
Animals may carry or transmit infection without clear clinical signs.
The guidance includes incident-management, communication and contact-assessment material.
Non-toxigenic C. ulcerans in animals does not require the same public-health follow-up.
A suspected zoonotic source requires confirmatory laboratory and epidemiological evidence before attribution.
